To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority of trigeminal neurons encode the kinematic parameters of active whisker movements in the rat, but not in a manner that is time-locked to movement initiation.

(1) many, but not all, trigeminal ganglia neurons respond to whisker movements in a manner that is correlated with a kinematic parameter and that (2) the responses of a subset of trigeminal neurons represent kinematics in a highly reliable manner.

1) the vast majority of trigeminal afferent neurons encode kinematic information, but that the majority of these neurons do not do so reliably; 2) the majority of these kinematic neurons are tuned to whisker movement direction; 3) the tuning of kinematic neurons to movement direction is modulated by amplitude and speed; 4) the kinematic responses are temporally dispersed and not time-locked.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the brain encodes information about the sensory world.
how the brain encodes the kinematics of self-generated whisking in the absence of any sensory feedback.

the majority ( approximately70%) of trigeminally innervated whisker follicle mechanoreceptors respond to whisker movement in air, and a subset ( approximately30%) represent whisker movements with high reliability.

trigeminal ganglia neurons are not well suited to represent kinematics, but that some neurons can be used to represent the direction of whisker movements in a reliable manner, although the time of occurrence is not well defined.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the trigeminal ganglia encode the kinematics, but not the dynamics, of whisker movements.
, although the trigeminal ganglia encode the kinematics, the temporal pattern of the neural responses is more complex than that of the whisker kinematics.
trigeminal ganglia neurons do not encode whisker kinematics with the precision and specificity of the sensory responses, although they do represent whisker movements with some reliability.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the trigeminal ganglia are capable of representing kinematic parameters of the whisker's motion, and thus may play a role in active sensing.
whisker movements in the absence of contacts are not encoded by trigeminal neurons in a simple manner, but rather are encoded in an idiosyncratic manner that varies across neurons.
the trigeminal ganglia are not simply sensory organs but also encode the kinematics and dynamics of whisker movement.
